issues.legal_issue: A witness’s testimony is not wholly excluded merely because the prosecution has declared the witness hostile, and portions supporting the prosecution may be relied on when corroborated by reliable evidence.
material_facts: Three witnesses were declared hostile, but their testimony supported the occurrence of a dacoity, the deceased’s serious injuries, and the presence of witnesses at or near the scene.
The prosecution also relied on eyewitness and injured-witness testimony, supported by medical evidence and the surrounding circumstances.
issues.conclusion: The hostile witnesses’ evidence was admissible and could be relied on to the extent that it supported the prosecution and was corroborated by other reliable evidence.
issues.legal_principle: Section 154 of the Evidence Act permits a party, with the court’s leave, to cross-examine its own witness. A hostile witness’s testimony is not erased from the record; the court may rely on portions supporting the prosecution if corroborated by reliable evidence. The Court relied on Bhajju @ Karan v. State of Madhya Pradesh (2012) 4 SCC 327, which discusses Koli Lakhmanbhai Chanabhai v. State of Gujarat (1999) 8 SCC 624, Prithi v. State of Haryana (2010) 8 SCC 536, Sidhartha Vashisht @ Manu Sharma v. State (NCT of Delhi) (2010) 6 SCC 1, and Ramkrushna v. State of Maharashtra (2007) 13 SCC 525.

rule.if: criminal_trial and witness_declared_hostile and testimony_supports_prosecution and corroborated_by_reliable_evidence

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.witness_declared_hostile: The prosecution asked the court to treat a witness as hostile, and the court did so.
predicates.testimony_supports_prosecution: Part of the witness’s testimony supports the prosecution’s account of the incident.
predicates.corroborated_by_reliable_evidence: Other reliable evidence supports the relevant part of the witness’s testimony.

issues.definition: When a witness is declared hostile in a criminal trial, a supporting part of the testimony may be relied on if other reliable evidence corroborates it.

issues.legal_issue: A witness’s relationship to the victim does not, by itself, make the witness’s testimony unreliable, particularly where the witness was naturally present or injured and the testimony is supported by other evidence.
material_facts: The eyewitnesses were members of the deceased’s family and were present in the house at the time of the nighttime attack.
Two of the principal witnesses had been injured, and witnesses identified the appellant during the incident.
Medical and other evidence supported the account of the attack and the injuries.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ close relationship to the deceased did not justify rejecting their testimony; their presence and accounts were credible in light of their injuries and the corroborating evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the credibility of the witnesses in light of their natural presence, the injuries suffered by two of them, the consistency of their accounts under cross-examination, and corroboration from medical and other evidence. It stated that relationship alone is not a sufficient ground to discard testimony; no specific earlier case was cited for this proposition in the Court’s discussion.

rule.if: criminal_trial and eyewitness_related_to_victim and (eyewitness_injured or presence_at_scene_natural) and testimony_corroborated

predicates.criminal_trial: The proceeding is a criminal trial.
predicates.eyewitness_related_to_victim: An eyewitness is related to the victim.
predicates.eyewitness_injured: The eyewitness sustained injuries during the incident.
predicates.presence_at_scene_natural: The eyewitness’s presence at the scene is natural in the circumstances.
predicates.testimony_corroborated: Other evidence supports the eyewitness’s testimony.

issues.definition: In a criminal trial, relationship to the victim alone does not discredit an eyewitness’s testimony when the witness was injured or naturally present and the testimony is corroborated.

issues.legal_issue: The acquittal of some alleged members of an unlawful assembly does not automatically prevent conviction of another participant under constructive liability where the prosecution proves the required assembly and the accused’s participation beyond reasonable doubt.
material_facts: The prosecution alleged that five miscreants participated in the nighttime attack.
The trial court acquitted three accused because they had not been identified and direct evidence against them was lacking; the State did not challenge those acquittals.
The appellant was identified by eyewitnesses, including an injured witness, and the evidence attributed fatal injuries to him.
issues.conclusion: The acquittals of the other accused did not, by themselves, vitiate the appellant’s conviction under Section 302/149 IPC; the Court also held that direct evidence established the appellant’s liability for murder under Section 302 IPC.
issues.legal_principle: Section 149 IPC imposes constructive liability on members of an unlawful assembly for an offence committed in pursuit of the assembly’s common object, provided the relevant assembly and the accused’s membership are proved. The Court stated that where five or more persons are charged and the prosecution proves its case beyond reasonable doubt against some, the failure to prove identification, role, or object as to others does not necessarily prevent conviction of those proved participants. It relied on Khem Karan v. State of U.P., AIR 1974 SC 1567, which applied constructive liability in considering an offence under Section 307 read with Section 149 IPC.

rule.if: prosecution_for_unlawful_assembly_offence and assembly_of_five_or_more_proved and accused_participation_proved_beyond_reasonable_doubt and some_coaccused_acquitted

predicates.prosecution_for_unlawful_assembly_offenc: The proceeding prosecutes an accused for an offence based on participation in an unlawful assembly.
predicates.assembly_of_five_or_more_proved: The evidence establishes an unlawful assembly consisting of at least five persons.
predicates.accused_participation_proved_beyond_reas: The prosecution proves beyond reasonable doubt that the accused participated in the relevant assembly and offence.
predicates.some_coaccused_acquitted: One or more other accused alleged to have participated in the assembly are acquitted.

issues.definition: An acquittal of some alleged assembly members does not bar conviction of a participant whose own participation is proved, when the evidence establishes the required assembly.

issues.legal_issue: Joint participants in nighttime lurking house-trespass or housebreaking may incur constructive liability when one of them causes death or grievous hurt, without proof that they shared a common intention or object; the person who actually causes the death may be punished for murder.
material_facts: The accused were charged and tried for an offence involving lurking house-trespass or housebreaking by night, as well as for offences involving the death and injuries caused during the incident.
The evidence identified the appellant as a participant who inflicted fatal injuries on the deceased.
The Court found that the fatal injuries were intentionally inflicted on vital parts and that the direct evidence supported the appellant’s liability for murder.
issues.conclusion: The Court held that common intention or common object need not be proved to establish the constructive liability described in Section 460 IPC. The appellant’s direct responsibility for the fatal injuries independently supported his conviction for murder under Section 302 IPC.
issues.legal_principle: Section 460 IPC applies where persons are jointly concerned in lurking house-trespass by night or housebreaking by night and one of them voluntarily causes or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt. The Court characterized this as constructive, not contributory, liability and stated that proof of common intention or common object is unnecessary if joint participation in the specified conduct is established. The person who actually causes death or grievous hurt remains liable under the relevant substantive offence. The Court relied on Abdul Aziz v. State of Rajasthan (2007) 10 SCC 283 concerning the liability of a person who commits murder while committing housebreaking by night.

predicates.night_housebreaking_case: The proceeding concerns lurking house-trespass by night or housebreaking by night.
predicates.participants_acted_jointly: The accused persons jointly participated in the specified nighttime trespass or housebreaking.
predicates.death_or_grievous_hurt_caused_by_partici: One of the participants voluntarily caused or attempted to cause death or grievous hurt during that conduct.

issues.definition: When persons jointly participate in the specified nighttime trespass or housebreaking and one causes or attempts to cause death or grievous hurt, the joint participants may incur constructive liability for that result.
